claim: The cerebellar granule cell layer has inspired numerous theoretical models of neural representations that support learned behaviors, beginning with the work of Marr and Albus.
source: The cerebellar granule cell layer has inspired numerous theoretical models of neural representations that support learned behaviors, beginning with the work of Marr and Albus.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Marr (1969) and Albus (1971) in the manuscript.

claim: In theoretical models, granule cells form a sparse, combinatorial encoding of diverse sensorimotor inputs.
source: In these models, granule cells form a sparse, combinatorial encoding of diverse sensorimotor inputs.
evidence: This is a description of theoretical models cited in the manuscript.

claim: Sparse representations are optimal for learning to discriminate random stimuli.
source: Such sparse representations are optimal for learning to discriminate random stimuli.
evidence: This is stated as a property of sparse representations in the context of theoretical models.

claim: Recent observations have shown dense, low-dimensional activity across granule cells.
source: However, recent observations of dense, low-dimensional activity across granule cells have called into question the role of sparse coding in these neurons.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to experimental studies (Jörntell and Ekerot, 2006; Knogler et al., 2017; Wagner et al., 2017; Giovannucci et al., 2017; Badura and De Zeeuw, 2017; Wagner et al., 2019).

claim: For continuous input-output transformations required for smooth motor control, the optimal granule cell representation is substantially denser than predicted by classical theories.
source: We show that for such tasks, the optimal granule cell representation is substantially denser than predicted by classical theories.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Optimal cerebellar representations are task-dependent.
source: Our results provide a general theory of learning in cerebellum-like systems and suggest that optimal cerebellar representations are task-dependent.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study, supported by data across multiple figures showing different optimal coding levels for different tasks.

claim: The cerebellar cortex exhibits a vast expansion in number of granule cells compared to the mossy fibers that innervate them.
source: A striking property of cerebellar anatomy is the vast expansion in number of granule cells compared to the mossy fibers that innervate them (Eccles et al., 1967).
evidence: This anatomical fact is supported by citation to Eccles et al., 1967.

claim: The function of the granule cell layer is to produce a high-dimensional representation of lower-dimensional mossy fiber activity.
source: This anatomical feature has led to the proposal that the function of the granule cell layer is to produce a high-dimensional representation of lower-dimensional mossy fiber activity (Marr, 1969; Albus, 1971; Cayco-Gajic and Silver, 2019).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal supported by citations.

claim: Granule cells integrate information from multiple mossy fibers and respond in a nonlinear manner to different input combinations.
source: In such theories, granule cells integrate information from multiple mossy fibers and respond in a nonlinear manner to different input combinations.
evidence: This describes a property of granule cells in theoretical models.

claim: The ratio of granule cells to mossy fibers has quantitative values that maximize the dimension of the granule cell representation and learning capacity.
source: Detailed theoretical analysis has argued that anatomical parameters such as the ratio of granule cells to mossy fibers (Babadi and Sompolinsky, 2014), the number of inputs received by individual granule cells (Litwin-Kumar et al., 2017; Cayco-Gajic et al., 2017), and the distribution of granule-cell-to-Purkinje-cell synaptic weights Brunel et al., 2004 have quantitative values that maximize the dimension of the granule cell representation and learning capacity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical studies.

claim: Sparse activity increases the dimension of granule cell representations.
source: Sparse activity, which increases dimension, is also cited as a key property of this representation (Marr, 1969; Albus, 1971; Babadi and Sompolinsky, 2014; but see Spanne and Jörntell, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: Sparsity affects both learning speed and generalization.
source: Sparsity affects both learning speed (Cayco-Gajic et al., 2017) and generalization, the ability to predict correct labels for previously unseen inputs (Barak et al., 2013; Babadi and Sompolinsky, 2014; Litwin-Kumar et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Previous theories studying the effects of dimension on learning typically focus on categorization tasks with random, high-dimensional inputs.
source: Theories that study the effects of dimension on learning typically focus on the ability of a system to perform categorization tasks with random, high-dimensional inputs (Barak et al., 2013; Babadi and Sompolinsky, 2014; Litwin-Kumar et al., 2017; Cayco-Gajic et al., 2017).
evidence: This characterizes previous theoretical work with citations.

claim: Increasing the dimension of the granule cell representation increases the number of inputs that can be discriminated in random categorization tasks.
source: In this case, increasing the dimension of the granule cell representation increases the number of inputs that can be discriminated.
evidence: This is a property of high-dimensional representations in the context of categorization tasks.

claim: Cerebellar circuits participate in diverse behaviors, including dexterous movements, inter-limb coordination, the formation of internal models, and cognitive behaviors.
source: However, cerebellar circuits participate in diverse behaviors, including dexterous movements, inter-limb coordination, the formation of internal models, and cognitive behaviors (Ito and Itō, 1984; Wolpert et al., 1998; Strick et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental and review literature.

claim: Cerebellum-like circuits support functions such as associative learning and the cancellation of self-generated sensory signals.
source: Cerebellum-like circuits, such as the insect mushroom body and the electrosensory system of electric fish, support other functions such as associative learning (Modi et al., 2020) and the cancellation of self-generated sensory signals (Kennedy et al., 2014), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on cerebellum-like structures.

claim: Several recent studies have reported dense activity in cerebellar granule cells in response to sensory stimulation or during motor control tasks.
source: Several recent studies have reported dense activity in cerebellar granule cells in response to sensory stimulation or during motor control tasks (Jörntell and Ekerot, 2006; Knogler et al., 2017; Wagner et al., 2017; Giovannucci et al., 2017; Badura and De Zeeuw, 2017; Wagner et al., 2019), at odds with classical theories (Marr, 1969; Albus, 1971).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: There is evidence that granule cell firing rates differ across cerebellar regions.
source: Moreover, there is evidence that granule cell firing rates differ across cerebellar regions (Heath et al., 2014; Witter and De Zeeuw, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Odor responses in Kenyon cells are sparse, with 5–10% of neurons responding to odor stimulation.
source: In contrast to this reported dense activity in cerebellar granule cells, odor responses in Kenyon cells, the analogs of granule cells in the Drosophila mushroom body, are sparse, with 5–10% of neurons responding to odor stimulation (Turner et al., 2008; Honegger et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies on Drosophila.

claim: Differences in coding levels across cerebellum-like systems can be explained by the capacity of representations with different levels of sparsity to support learning of different tasks.
source: We propose that these differences can be explained by the capacity of representations with different levels of sparsity to support learning of different tasks.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their theoretical analysis.

claim: When learning input-output mappings for motor control tasks, the optimal granule cell representation is much denser than predicted by previous analyses.
source: We show that the optimal level of sparsity depends on the structure of the input-output relationship of a task. When learning input-output mappings for motor control tasks, the optimal granule cell representation is much denser than predicted by previous analyses.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by simulation data in Figure 2F.

claim: Properties of cerebellar architecture and activity control these networks' inductive bias.
source: The theory describes how properties of cerebellar architecture and activity control these networks' inductive bias: the tendency of a network toward learning particular types of input-output mappings (Sollich, 1998; Jacot et al., 2018; Bordelon et al., 2020; Canatar et al., 2021b; Simon et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a theoretical result of the study, with citations to related work on inductive bias.

claim: Inductive bias, rather than the dimension of the representation alone, is necessary to explain learning performance across tasks.
source: The theory shows that inductive bias, rather than the dimension of the representation alone, is necessary to explain learning performance across tasks.
evidence: This is a key theoretical insight from the study, supported by the analysis in Figure 4.

claim: Cerebellar regions specialized for different functions may adjust the sparsity of their granule cell representations depending on the task.
source: It also suggests that cerebellar regions specialized for different functions may adjust the sparsity of their granule cell representations depending on the task.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the theoretical findings of the study.

claim: A typical assumption in computational theories of the cerebellar cortex is that inputs are randomly distributed in a high-dimensional space.
source: A typical assumption in computational theories of the cerebellar cortex is that inputs are randomly distributed in a high-dimensional space (Marr, 1969; Albus, 1971; Brunel et al., 2004; Babadi and Sompolinsky, 2014; Billings et al., 2014; Litwin-Kumar et al., 2017).
evidence: This characterizes assumptions in previous theoretical work, supported by citations.

claim: Many tasks, including cerebellum-dependent tasks, are likely best-described as being encoded by a low-dimensional set of variables.
source: While this may be a reasonable simplification in some cases, many tasks, including cerebellum-dependent tasks, are likely best-described as being encoded by a low-dimensional set of variables.
evidence: This is a reasoning about the nature of cerebellar tasks that motivates the model design.

claim: The cerebellum is often hypothesized to learn a forward model for motor control.
source: For example, the cerebellum is often hypothesized to learn a forward model for motor control (Wolpert et al., 1998), which uses sensory input and motor efference to predict an effector's future state.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about cerebellar function supported by citation.

claim: Mossy fiber activity recorded in monkeys correlates with position and velocity during natural movement.
source: Mossy fiber activity recorded in monkeys correlates with position and velocity during natural movement (van Kan et al., 1993).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by citation.

claim: Motor cortex population activity lies on a low-dimensional manifold.
source: Sources of motor efference copies include motor cortex, whose population activity lies on a low-dimensional manifold (Wagner et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2013; Churchland et al., 2010; Yu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by citations.

claim: For random categorization tasks, performance is maximized at low coding levels.
source: For random categorization tasks, performance is maximized at low coding levels (Figure 2E), consistent with previous results (Barak et al., 2013; Babadi and Sompolinsky, 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in Figure 2E, consistent with previous theoretical work.

claim: For continuously varying outputs, the optimal coding level depends strongly on the length scale, with learning performance for slowly varying functions optimized at much higher coding levels than quickly varying functions.
source: For continuously varying outputs, the dependence is qualitatively different (Figure 2F). The optimal coding level depends strongly on the length scale, with learning performance for slowly varying functions optimized at much higher coding levels than quickly varying functions.
evidence: This is a primary finding from simulations shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The dependence of optimal coding level on length scale holds for different choices of threshold-nonlinear functions.
source: This dependence holds for different choices of threshold-nonlinear functions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) or input dimension (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) and is most pronounced when the number of training patterns is limited (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by simulation data in supplementary figures.

claim: The observations are at odds with previous theories of the role of sparse granule cell representations.
source: Our observations are at odds with previous theories of the role of sparse granule cell representations (Marr, 1969; Albus, 1971; Babadi and Sompolinsky, 2014; Billings et al., 2014) and show that sparse activity does not always optimize performance for this broader set of tasks.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in relation to previous theories.

claim: As the coding level is reduced, the overlap between representations of different inputs is also reduced.
source: As the coding level is reduced, this overlap is also reduced (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The reduction in overlap is greater than the reduction in number of neurons that respond to either of the individual inputs, reflecting the fact that representations with low coding levels perform 'pattern separation'.
source: In fact, this reduction in overlap is greater than the reduction in number of neurons that respond to either of the individual inputs, reflecting the fact that representations with low coding levels perform 'pattern separation' (Figure 3B, compare purple and red or blue regions).
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 3B with an interpretation about pattern separation.

claim: The kernel of the network measures overlap of representations in the expansion layer as a function of the task variables.
source: This effect is summarized by the 'kernel' of the network (Schölkopf and Smola, 2002; Rahimi and Recht, 2007), which measures overlap of representations in the expansion layer as a function of the task variables
evidence: This defines the kernel function used in the analysis, with citations to relevant literature.

claim: Representations with lower coding levels exhibit greater pattern separation.
source: Plotting the kernel for different choices of coding level demonstrates that representations with lower coding levels exhibit greater pattern separation (Figure 3C; Babadi and Sompolinsky, 2014).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C and is consistent with previous work.

claim: Decreasing the coding level increases the dimension of the representation.
source: This is consistent with the observation that decreasing the coding level increases the dimension of the representation (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D.

claim: For high-dimensional, random categorization tasks, performance depends only on overlaps at two spatial scales: the overlap between training patterns belonging to different clusters, which is small, and the overlap between training and test patterns belonging to the same cluster, which is large.
source: In this case, performance depends only on overlaps at two spatial scales: the overlap between training patterns belonging to different clusters, which is small, and the overlap between training and test patterns belonging to the same cluster, which is large (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an analytical result about the structure of random categorization tasks, illustrated in Figure 4B.

claim: Sparse expansion layer representations reduce the overlap of patterns belonging to different clusters, increasing dimension and generalization performance.
source: Sparse expansion layer representations reduce the overlap of patterns belonging to different clusters, increasing dimension and generalization performance (Figure 3D, Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 3D and 2E.

claim: Coding level substantially changes the frequency dependence of the eigenvalues associated with spherical harmonic eigenfunctions.
source: We find that coding level substantially changes the frequency dependence of the eigenvalues associated with these eigenfunctions (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Higher coding levels increase the relative magnitude of the low frequency eigenvalues compared to high-frequency eigenvalues.
source: Higher coding levels increase the relative magnitude of the low frequency eigenvalues compared to high-frequency eigenvalues.
evidence: This is an observation from the eigenvalue analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Increasing length scale in Gaussian process targets corresponds to a greater relative contribution of low versus high frequency modes.
source: For the Gaussian process targets, we have considered, increasing length scale corresponds to a greater relative contribution of low versus high frequency modes (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The optima observed in Figure 2F are a consequence of the difference in eigenvalues of networks with different coding levels.
source: Our theory reveals that the optima observed in Figure 2F are a consequence of the difference in eigenvalues of networks with different coding levels.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the theoretical results in relation to simulation data.

claim: Networks with low and high coding levels have an inductive bias toward the learning of high and low frequency functions, respectively.
source: This reflects an inductive bias (Sollich, 1998; Jacot et al., 2018; Bordelon et al., 2020; Canatar et al., 2021b; Simon et al., 2021) of networks with low and high coding levels toward the learning of high and low frequency functions, respectively (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation supported by data in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, with citations to related work.

claim: The coding level's effect on a network's inductive bias, rather than dimension alone, determines learning performance.
source: Thus, the coding level's effect on a network's inductive bias, rather than dimension alone, determines learning performance.
evidence: This is a key theoretical conclusion of the study.

claim: Previous studies that focused only on random categorization tasks did not observe the dependence of optimal coding level on task structure, since errors in such tasks are dominated by the learning of high frequency components, for which sparse activity is optimal.
source: Previous studies that focused only on random categorization tasks did not observe this dependence, since errors in such tasks are dominated by the learning of high frequency components, for which sparse activity is optimal (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an explanation for why previous studies reached different conclusions, supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: A desirable property of the expansion layer representation is that effective weights sample the space of task variables uniformly.
source: A desirable property of the expansion layer representation is that these effective weights sample the space of task variables uniformly (Figure 3A), increasing the heterogeneity of tuning of expansion layer neurons (Litwin-Kumar et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a theoretical property with citation to previous work.

claim: With a clustered representation, sparse connectivity dramatically reduces performance.
source: If, on the other hand, the input layer forms a clustered representation containing groups of neurons that each encode a single task variable (Figure 5D, bottom), we may expect different results. Indeed, with a clustered representation, sparse connectivity dramatically reduces performance (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The equivalence between sparse and fully connected networks validates the applicability of the theory to more realistic networks.
source: This equivalence validates the applicability of our theory to these more realistic networks.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings about sparse connectivity.

claim: The results argue for the importance of distributed sensorimotor representations in the cortico-cerebellar pathway.
source: It also argues for the importance of distributed sensorimotor representations in the cortico-cerebellar pathway, consistent with the distributed nature of representations in motor cortex (Shenoy et al., 2013; Muscinelli et al., 2023).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings with citations to related work.

claim: A history of theoretical modeling has shown a remarkable correspondence between anatomical properties of the cerebellar cortex and model parameters optimal for learning.
source: A history of theoretical modeling has shown a remarkable correspondence between anatomical properties of the cerebellar cortex and model parameters optimal for learning.
evidence: This is a characterization of previous theoretical work.

claim: The optimal in-degree is small for all the tasks considered in the study.
source: The optimal in-degree is small for all the tasks we consider, suggesting that sparse connectivity is sufficient for high performance across a range of tasks (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The distribution of granule-cell-to-Purkinje cell synaptic weights is consistent with the distribution that maximizes the number of random binary input-output mappings stored.
source: Brunel et al., 2004 showed that the distribution of granule-cell-to-Purkinje cell synaptic weights is consistent with the distribution that maximizes the number of random binary input-output mappings stored.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brunel et al., 2004.

claim: The distribution of granule-cell-to-Purkinje cell weights exhibits a substantial fraction of silent synapses, consistent with experiments.
source: This distribution exhibits a substantial fraction of silent synapses, consistent with experiments.
evidence: This is a property of the weight distribution that is consistent with experimental observations.

claim: A similar weight distribution with a substantial fraction of silent synapses holds for tasks where targets are a smoothly varying function of task variables.
source: However, the case we consider, where targets are a smoothly varying function of task variables, has not been explored. We observe a similar weight distribution for these tasks (Figure 6C), with the fraction of silent synapses remaining high across coding levels (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 6C and 6D.

claim: The fraction of silent synapses is lower for networks learning Gaussian process targets than those learning random categorization tasks.
source: The fraction of silent synapses is lower for networks learning Gaussian process targets than those learning random categorization tasks, consistent with the capacity of a given network for learning such targets being larger (Clopath et al., 2012).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D and is consistent with previous theoretical work.

claim: Optimal coding level is task-dependent, but optimal architectural parameters are largely task-independent.
source: Although optimal coding level is task-dependent, these analyses suggest that optimal architectural parameters are largely task-independent.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analyses in Figure 6.

claim: Coding level tunes the inductive bias of the network to favor the learning of specific tasks.
source: Whereas coding level tunes the inductive bias of the network to favor the learning of specific tasks, these architectural parameters control properties of the representation that improve performance across tasks.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings about coding level and architectural parameters.

claim: Sparse connectivity and a large expansion support uniform sampling of low-dimensional task variables.
source: In particular, sparse connectivity and a large expansion support uniform sampling of low-dimensional task variables (consistent with Figure 5C), while a large fraction of silent synapses is a consequence of a readout that maximizes learning performance (Brunel et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings with citation to previous work.

claim: For learning the dynamics of a two-joint arm, performance is optimized at substantially higher coding levels than for random categorization tasks.
source: To model the cerebellum's role in predicting the consequences of motor commands (Wolpert et al., 1998), we examined the optimal coding level for learning the dynamics of a two-joint arm (Fagg et al., 1997). Given an initial state, the network predicts the change in the future position of the arm (Figure 7A). Performance is optimized at substantially higher coding levels than for random categorization tasks, consistent with our previous results for continuous input-output mappings (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A and is consistent with previous results.

claim: The optimal coding level in a model of the Drosophila mushroom body for odor categorization is less than 0.1.
source: The mushroom body, a cerebellum-like structure in insects, is required for learning of associations between odors and appetitive or aversive valence (Modi et al., 2020). This behavior can be represented as a mapping from random representations of odors in the input layer to binary category labels (Figure 7B). The optimal coding level in a model with parameters consistent with the Drosophila mushroom body is less than 0.1, consistent with our previous results for random categorization tasks (Figure 2E) and the sparse odor-evoked responses in Drosophila Kenyon cells (Turner et al., 2008; Honegger et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B and is consistent with experimental observations.

claim: In a model of the electrosensory lateral line lobe, the coding level corresponding to biophysical parameters estimated from data coincided with the value at which further increases in performance were modest.
source: The prediction and cancellation of self-generated sensory feedback has been studied extensively in mormyrid weakly electric fish and depends on the electrosensory lateral line lobe (ELL), a cerebellum-like structure (Bell et al., 2008). Granule cells in the ELL provide a temporal basis for generating negative images that are used to cancel self-generated feedback (Figure 7C). We extended a detailed model of granule cells and their inputs (Kennedy et al., 2014) to study the influence of coding level on the effectiveness of this basis. The performance of this model saturated at relatively high coding levels, and notably the coding level corresponding to biophysical parameters estimated from data coincided with the value at which further increases in performance were modest.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C.

claim: For learning VOR tuning curves, performance is high across a range of coding levels and sparse codes are sufficient (although not necessary).
source: A canonical function of the mammalian cerebellum is the adjustment of the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR), in which motion of the head is detected and triggers compensatory ocular motion in the opposite direction. During VOR learning, Purkinje cells are tuned to head velocity, and their tuning curves are described as piecewise linear functions (Lisberger et al., 1994; Figure 7D). Although in vivo population recordings of granule cells during VOR adaptation are not, to our knowledge, available for comparison, our model predicts that performance for learning such tuning curves is high across a range of coding levels and shows that sparse codes are sufficient (although not necessary) for such tasks (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The model predicts diverse coding levels across different behaviors dependent on cerebellum-like structures.
source: These results predict diverse coding levels across different behaviors dependent on cerebellum-like structures.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the results shown in Figure 7.

claim: The odor categorization and VOR tasks both have input-output mappings that exhibit sharp nonlinearities and can be efficiently learned using sparse representations.
source: The odor categorization and VOR tasks both have input-output mappings that exhibit sharp nonlinearities and can be efficiently learned using sparse representations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results for these specific tasks.

claim: The forward modeling and feedback cancellation tasks have smooth input-output mappings and exhibit denser optima.
source: In contrast, the forward modeling and feedback cancellation tasks have smooth input-output mappings and exhibit denser optima.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results for these specific tasks.

claim: While sparse representations are suitable for learning to categorize inputs into random categories, as predicted by classic theories, tasks involving structured input-output mappings benefit from denser representations.
source: We have shown that the optimal granule cell coding level depends on the task being learned. While sparse representations are suitable for learning to categorize inputs into random categories, as predicted by classic theories, tasks involving structured input-output mappings benefit from denser representations (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: The findings reconcile classic theories with the observation of dense granule cell activation during movement.
source: This reconciles such theories with the observation of dense granule cell activation during movement (Knogler et al., 2017; Wagner et al., 2017; Giovannucci et al., 2017; Badura and De Zeeuw, 2017; Wagner et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an interpretation of how the findings relate to experimental observations.

claim: In contrast to the task-dependence of optimal coding level, optimal anatomical values of granule cell and Purkinje cell connectivity are largely task-independent.
source: We also show that, in contrast to the task-dependence of optimal coding level, optimal anatomical values of granule cell and Purkinje cell connectivity are largely task-independent (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a summary of findings shown in Figure 6.

claim: A stereotyped cerebellar architecture may support diverse representations optimized for a variety of learning tasks.
source: This distinction suggests that a stereotyped cerebellar architecture may support diverse representations optimized for a variety of learning tasks.
evidence: This is an interpretation and implication of the findings.

claim: In random categorization tasks with random, high-dimensional inputs, a low coding level increases the dimension of the granule cell representation, permitting more associations to be stored and improving generalization to previously unseen inputs.
source: In this case, a low coding level increases the dimension of the granule cell representation, permitting more associations to be stored and improving generalization to previously unseen inputs.
evidence: This is a characterization of how sparse coding benefits random categorization tasks.

claim: The optimal coding level is low but not arbitrarily low, as extremely sparse representations introduce noise that hinders generalization.
source: The optimal coding level is low but not arbitrarily low, as extremely sparse representations introduce noise that hinders generalization (Barak et al., 2013; Babadi and Sompolinsky, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: The learning problems in this study extend previous studies by considering inputs that may be constrained to a low-dimensional task subspace, input-output mappings beyond random categorization tasks, and generalization error for arbitrary locations on the task subspace.
source: To examine a broader family of tasks, our learning problems extend previous studies in several ways. First, we consider inputs that may be constrained to a low-dimensional task subspace. Second, we consider input-output mappings beyond random categorization tasks. Finally, we assess generalization error for arbitrary locations on the task subspace, rather than only for noisy instances of previously presented inputs.
evidence: This describes how the current study extends previous work.

claim: The analysis generalizes previous approaches that focused on dimension and noise alone.
source: Our analysis generalizes previous approaches (Barak et al., 2013; Babadi and Sompolinsky, 2014; Litwin-Kumar et al., 2017) that focused on dimension and noise alone.
evidence: This is a characterization of how the current analysis relates to previous work.

claim: Both dimension and noise for random patterns can be directly calculated from the kernel function.
source: In particular, both dimension and noise for random patterns can be directly calculated from the kernel function (Figure 3C; see Appendix).
evidence: This is a theoretical result of the study.

claim: The theory builds upon techniques that have been developed for understanding properties of kernel regression.
source: Our theory builds upon techniques that been developed for understanding properties of kernel regression (Sollich, 1998; Jacot et al., 2018; Bordelon et al., 2020; Canatar et al., 2021b; Simon et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to related work.

claim: This is the first kernel study of the effects of nonzero average thresholds.
source: Prior studies have analyzed kernels corresponding to networks with zero (Cho and Saul, 2010) or mean-zero Gaussian thresholds (Basri et al., 2019; Jacot et al., 2018), which in both cases produce networks with a coding level of 0.5. Ours is the first kernel study of the effects of nonzero average thresholds.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study with citations to previous work.

claim: The full characterization of the eigenvalue spectra and their decay rates as a function of the threshold extends previous work.
source: Our full characterization of the eigenvalue spectra and their decay rates as a function of the threshold extends previous work (Bach, 2017; Bietti and Bach, 2021).
evidence: This is a claim about the contribution of the study with citations to previous work.

claim: Artificial neural network studies typically assume either fully-connected or convolutional layers, yet pruning connections after training barely degrades performance.
source: Furthermore, artificial neural network studies typically assume either fully-connected or convolutional layers, yet pruning connections after training barely degrades performance (Han et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on neural network pruning.

claim: The results support the idea that sparsely connected networks may behave like dense ones if the representation is distributed.
source: Our results support the idea that sparsely connected networks may behave like dense ones if the representation is distributed (Figure 5), providing insight into the regimes in which pruning preserves performance.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in relation to neural network pruning.

claim: Other studies have considered tasks with smooth input-output mappings and low-dimensional inputs, finding that heterogeneous Golgi cell inhibition can improve performance by diversifying individual granule cell thresholds.
source: Other studies have considered tasks with smooth input-output mappings and low-dimensional inputs, finding that heterogeneous Golgi cell inhibition can improve performance by diversifying individual granule cell thresholds (Spanne and Jörntell, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Another proposal states that dense coding may improve generalization.
source: Another proposal states that dense coding may improve generalization (Spanne and Jörntell, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The theory reveals that whether or not dense coding is beneficial depends on the task.
source: Our theory reveals that whether or not dense coding is beneficial depends on the task.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the theoretical analysis.

claim: The theory assumes that inputs are normalized and distributed uniformly in a linear subspace of the input layer activity.
source: When comparing the inductive biases of networks with different coding levels, our theory assumes that inputs are normalized and distributed uniformly in a linear subspace of the input layer activity.
evidence: This describes an assumption of the theoretical model.

claim: A similar analysis can be performed when inputs are not uniformly distributed, but in this case the basis is determined by an interplay between this distribution and the nonlinearity of expansion layer neurons, making the analysis more complex.
source: A similar analysis can be performed when inputs are not uniformly distributed, but in this case the basis is determined by an interplay between this distribution and the nonlinearity of expansion layer neurons, making the analysis more complex (see Appendix).
evidence: This describes a potential extension of the analysis.

claim: The theory assumes that generalization is assessed for inputs drawn from the same distribution as used for learning.
source: We have also assumed that generalization is assessed for inputs drawn from the same distribution as used for learning.
evidence: This describes an assumption of the model.

claim: When analyzing properties of the granule cell layer, the theory assumes an infinitely wide expansion.
source: When analyzing properties of the granule cell layer, our theory also assumes an infinitely wide expansion.
evidence: This describes an assumption of the theoretical model.

claim: The theory does not explicitly model inhibitory input provided by Golgi cells, instead assuming such input can be modeled as a change in effective threshold.
source: We also have not explicitly modeled inhibitory input provided by Golgi cells, instead assuming such input can be modeled as a change in effective threshold, as in previous studies (Billings et al., 2014; Cayco-Gajic et al., 2017; Litwin-Kumar et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes an assumption of the model with citations to previous work.

claim: A key assumption concerning the granule cells is that they sample mossy fiber inputs randomly, as is typically assumed in Marr-Albus models.
source: Another key assumption concerning the granule cells is that they sample mossy fiber inputs randomly, as is typically assumed in Marr-Albus models (Marr, 1969; Albus, 1971; Litwin-Kumar et al., 2017; Cayco-Gajic et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes an assumption of the model with citations to previous work.

claim: Other studies argue that granule cells sample from mossy fibers with highly similar receptive fields.
source: Other studies instead argue that granule cells sample from mossy fibers with highly similar receptive fields (Garwicz et al., 1998; Brown and Bower, 2001; Jörntell and Ekerot, 2006) defined by the tuning of mossy fiber and climbing fiber inputs to cerebellar microzones (Apps et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: An alternative hypothesis is that granule cells serve to relay similarly tuned mossy fiber inputs and enhance their signal-to-noise ratio.
source: This has led to an alternative hypothesis that granule cells serve to relay similarly tuned mossy fiber inputs and enhance their signal-to-noise ratio (Jörntell and Ekerot, 2006; Gilbert and Chris Miall, 2022) rather than to re-encode inputs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Another hypothesis is that granule cells enable Purkinje cells to learn piece-wise linear approximations of nonlinear functions.
source: Another hypothesis is that granule cells enable Purkinje cells to learn piece-wise linear approximations of nonlinear functions (Spanne and Jörntell, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Several recent studies support the existence of heterogeneous connectivity and selectivity of granule cells to multiple distinct inputs at the local scale.
source: However, several recent studies support the existence of heterogeneous connectivity and selectivity of granule cells to multiple distinct inputs at the local scale (Huang et al., 2013; Ishikawa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The deviation of the predicted dimension in models constrained by electron-microscopy data as compared to randomly wired models is modest.
source: Furthermore, the deviation of the predicted dimension in models constrained by electron-microscopy data as compared to randomly wired models is modest (Nguyen et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Topographically organized connectivity at the macroscopic scale may coexist with disordered connectivity at the local scale, allowing granule cells presynaptic to an individual Purkinje cell to sample heterogeneous combinations of the subset of sensorimotor signals relevant to the tasks that Purkinje cell participates in.
source: Thus, topographically organized connectivity at the macroscopic scale may coexist with disordered connectivity at the local scale, allowing granule cells presynaptic to an individual Purkinje cell to sample heterogeneous combinations of the subset of sensorimotor signals relevant to the tasks that Purkinje cell participates in.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about cerebellar connectivity based on the discussion of previous work.

claim: The optimality of dense codes for learning slowly varying tasks suggests that observations of a lack of mixing for such tasks are compatible with Marr-Albus models, as in this case nonlinear mixing is not required.
source: Finally, we note that the optimality of dense codes for learning slowly varying tasks in our theory suggests that observations of a lack of mixing (Jörntell and Ekerot, 2002) for such tasks are compatible with Marr-Albus models, as in this case nonlinear mixing is not required.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in relation to experimental observations.

claim: Coding level is quantified by the fraction of neurons that are above firing threshold.
source: We have quantified coding level by the fraction of neurons that are above firing threshold.
evidence: This describes how coding level is defined in the model.

claim: Granule cells have been shown to exhibit reliable burst responses to mossy fiber stimulation.
source: Granule cells have been shown to exhibit reliable burst responses to mossy fiber stimulation (Chadderton et al., 2004), motivating models using deterministic responses or sub-Poisson spiking variability.
evidence: This is supported by citation to an experimental study.

claim: The model assumes that Purkinje cell responses to granule cell input can be modeled as an optimal linear readout.
source: For the Purkinje cells, our model assumes that their responses to granule cell input can be modeled as an optimal linear readout.
evidence: This describes an assumption of the model.

claim: The model provides an upper bound to linear readout performance, a standard benchmark for the quality of a neural representation.
source: Our model therefore provides an upper bound to linear readout performance, a standard benchmark for the quality of a neural representation that does not require assumptions on the nature of climbing fiber-mediated plasticity, which is still debated.
evidence: This describes a property of the model.

claim: Electrophysiological studies have argued in favor of a linear approximation for Purkinje cell responses.
source: Electrophysiological studies have argued in favor of a linear approximation (Brunel et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: When an online climbing fiber-mediated learning rule is implemented, optimal coding levels are still task-dependent.
source: To improve the biological applicability of our model, we implemented an online climbing fiber-mediated learning rule and found that optimal coding levels are still task-dependent (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The results predict that qualitative differences in the coding levels of cerebellum-like systems, across brain regions or across species, reflect an optimization to distinct tasks.
source: Our results predict that qualitative differences in the coding levels of cerebellum-like systems, across brain regions or across species, reflect an optimization to distinct tasks (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the results shown in Figure 7.

claim: It is possible that differences in coding level arise from other physiological differences between systems.
source: However, it is also possible that differences in coding level arise from other physiological differences between systems.
evidence: This is an alternative explanation for differences in coding level.

claim: In the Drosophila mushroom body, random and sparse subsets of Kenyon cells are activated in response to odor stimulation, consistent with the model.
source: In the Drosophila mushroom body, which is required for associative learning of odor categories, random and sparse subsets of Kenyon cells are activated in response to odor stimulation, consistent with our model (Figure 7B; Turner et al., 2008; Honegger et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies and is consistent with model predictions.

claim: Heterogeneity in granule cell firing has been observed across cerebellar lobules, associated with both differences in intrinsic properties and mossy fiber input.
source: Within the cerebellar cortex, heterogeneity in granule cell firing has been observed across cerebellar lobules, associated with both differences in intrinsic properties (Heath et al., 2014) and mossy fiber input (Witter and De Zeeuw, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The model predicts that regions involved in behaviors with substantial low-dimensional structure may exhibit higher coding levels than regions involved in categorization or discrimination of high-dimensional stimuli.
source: Our model predicts that regions involved in behaviors with substantial low-dimensional structure, for example smooth motor control tasks, may exhibit higher coding levels than regions involved in categorization or discrimination of high-dimensional stimuli.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the theoretical findings.

claim: The model raises the possibility that individual brain regions may exhibit different coding levels at different moments in time, depending on immediate behavioral or task demands.
source: Our model also raises the possibility that individual brain regions may exhibit different coding levels at different moments in time, depending on immediate behavioral or task demands.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the theoretical findings.

claim: Multiple mechanisms could support the dynamic adjustment of coding level, including changes in mossy fiber input, Golgi cell inhibition, retrograde signaling from Purkinje cells, or unsupervised plasticity of mossy fiber-to-granule cell synapses.
source: Multiple mechanisms could support the dynamic adjustment of coding level, including changes in mossy fiber input (Ozden et al., 2012), Golgi cell inhibition (Eccles et al., 1966; Palay and Chan-Palay, 1974), retrograde signaling from Purkinje cells (Kreitzer and Regehr, 2001), or unsupervised plasticity of mossy fiber-to-granule cell synapses (Schweighofer et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on various mechanisms.

claim: A recent study demonstrated that local synaptic inhibition by Golgi cells controls the spiking threshold and hence the population coding level of cerebellar granule cells in mice.
source: A recent study demonstrated that local synaptic inhibition by Golgi cells controls the spiking threshold and hence the population coding level of cerebellar granule cells in mice (Fleming et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent experimental study.

claim: Granule cell responses to sensory stimuli are sparse when movement-related selectivity is controlled for.
source: Further, the authors observed that granule cell responses to sensory stimuli are sparse when movement-related selectivity is controlled for.
evidence: This is an observation from Fleming et al., 2022.

claim: Dense movement-related activity and sparse sensory-evoked activity are not incompatible.
source: This suggests that dense movement-related activity and sparse sensory-evoked activity are not incompatible.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings from Fleming et al., 2022.

claim: If coding level is task-optimized, the model predicts that manipulating coding level artificially will diminish performance.
source: If coding level is task-optimized, our model predicts that manipulating coding level artificially will diminish performance.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the theoretical findings.

claim: In the Drosophila mushroom body, disrupting feedback inhibition from the GABAergic anterior paired lateral neuron onto Kenyon cells increases coding level and impairs odor discrimination.
source: In the Drosophila mushroom body, disrupting feedback inhibition from the GABAergic anterior paired lateral neuron onto Kenyon cells increases coding level and impairs odor discrimination (Lin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to an experimental study.

claim: Blocking inhibition from Golgi cells onto granule cells results in denser granule cell population activity and impairs performance on an eye-blink conditioning task.
source: A recent study demonstrated that blocking inhibition from Golgi cells onto granule cells results in denser granule cell population activity and impairs performance on an eye-blink conditioning task (Fleming et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent experimental study.

claim: These examples demonstrate that increasing coding level during sensory discrimination tasks, for which sparse activity is optimal, impairs performance.
source: These examples demonstrate that increasing coding level during sensory discrimination tasks, for which sparse activity is optimal, impairs performance.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings cited.

claim: The theory predicts that decreasing coding level during a task for which dense activity is optimal, such as smooth motor control, would also impair performance.
source: Our theory predicts that decreasing coding level during a task for which dense activity is optimal, such as smooth motor control, would also impair performance.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the theoretical findings.

claim: Dense activity has been taken as evidence against theories of combinatorial coding in cerebellar granule cells.
source: While dense activity has been taken as evidence against theories of combinatorial coding in cerebellar granule cells (Knogler et al., 2017; Wagner et al., 2019), our theory suggests that the two are not incompatible.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The theory suggests that dense activity and combinatorial coding are not incompatible.
source: While dense activity has been taken as evidence against theories of combinatorial coding in cerebellar granule cells (Knogler et al., 2017; Wagner et al., 2019), our theory suggests that the two are not incompatible.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the theoretical findings.

claim: The coding level of cerebellum-like regions may be determined by behavioral demands and the nature of the input to granule-like layers.
source: Instead, the coding level of cerebellum-like regions may be determined by behavioral demands and the nature of the input to granule-like layers (Muscinelli et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study with citation to related work.

claim: Sparse coding has been cited as a key property of sensory representations in the cerebral cortex.
source: Sparse coding has also been cited as a key property of sensory representations in the cerebral cortex (Olshausen and Field, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Recent population recordings show that sensory cortical regions exhibit dense movement-related activity, much like in cerebellum.
source: However, recent population recordings show that such regions exhibit dense movement-related activity (Musall et al., 2019), much like in cerebellum.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent experimental study.

claim: It is possible that cerebrocortical areas also operate using inductive biases that are shaped by coding level in a similar manner to the model.
source: While the theory presented in this study does not account for the highly structured recurrent interactions that characterize cerebrocortical regions, it is possible that these areas also operate using inductive biases that are shaped by coding level in a similar manner to our model.
evidence: This is a speculation about the applicability of the findings to other brain regions.
